boundary_conditions.consequence_if_violated: The observed effects may not generalize to other medicinal plant species.
boundary_conditions.scope_text: This paper aimed to compare the content of compounds with antioxidant properties in four species of medicinal plants, rosemary, peppermint, lemon balm and sage grown under organic and conventional conditions in 2 consecutive years.

boundary_conditions.consequence_if_violated: Results may differ in other climates or soil conditions.
boundary_conditions.scope_text: The dry matter and vitamin C content was determined according to Polish Standards; carotenoids and polyphenols were analysed by high-performance liquid chromatography.

causal_claims.claim_text: Organic medicinal plants contained significantly more dry matter, vitamin C, phenolic acids and total flavonoids than the plants from conventional production.
causal_claims.counterevidence_notes: Conventional plants had significantly more carotenoids than organic ones, indicating a mixed effect depending on the compound.

mechanisms.description: Organic farming practices may alter plant secondary metabolism, leading to higher concentrations of certain bioactive compounds (e.g., phenolic acids, flavonoids) as a stress response, while conventional farming may increase carotenoid content due to different nutrient availability or growth conditions.
mechanisms.theoretical_framework: Plant defense theory (stress-induced synthesis of secondary metabolites)

parsed_response.methodology: The study compared organic and conventional production systems across four medicinal plant species over two consecutive years. Analytical methods included Polish Standards for dry matter and vitamin C, and HPLC for carotenoids and polyphenols. Statistical significance was reported but no effect sizes or detailed methods were provided in the abstract.
